problems.description: Two distinct channel-specification paths: subscribe/unsubscribe read `payload.channel`, while message targeting uses the top-level `channel` field — ambiguous API design that forces readers to track which field applies to which message type.

Channel validation is duplicated: the top-level `incoming.get("channel")` type check in _handle_message is separate from and redundant with the payload-level channel check inside the subscribe/unsubscribe branch.

Convention score 0.83; two violations reported in test_app.py (Classes should use PascalCase; Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE). Note the app.py diff itself is convention-clean — the violations live in the test file.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +32 concentrated in _handle_message and the /channels/ path parsing (`.removeprefix().removesuffix().rstrip()` chain) — the branching is growing but still contained.

strengths: Consolidates client-removal logic into `_remove_client`/`_remove_stale_clients`, eliminating the previously duplicated pop-and-clean blocks.
Extracts a `_json_response` static helper, removing header/body repetition across health and channel endpoints.
Respects existing patterns: same RLock discipline around shared state, same message envelope, same health_response return shape, consistent type hints.
Handles edge cases properly — URL-unquote of channel names, 404 for unknown channels, subscriber cleanup on disconnect and empty-channel removal.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean channel pub/sub extension that fits the NotificationServer architecture and refactors duplicated client-cleanup logic into shared helpers, with only minor API-design ambiguity (dual channel fields) and two test-file convention violations (score 0.83) as blemishes.

problems.description: Hand-rolled minimal Redis RESP pub/sub client instead of a well-tested library; _execute opens a fresh connection per call, and the listen() task has no reconnect logic, so a dropped subscription silently halts message delivery.

Silent fallback to InMemoryBroker on OSError mixes dev/degraded semantics into the production path: a Redis outage quietly switches to single-process pub/sub, losing cross-instance delivery with no opt-in flag or log.
InMemoryBroker.subscribers/clients/channel_members are class attributes (shared across instances) and publish() relies on the brittle getattr(callback, '__self__').client_count coupling.
Measurement-flagged convention violations in test_app.py: non-PascalCase class names and non-UPPER_CASE module-level constants (score 0.83).
The new broker/store surface (RESP parsing, fallback switching, SQLite listing) is added with no accompanying test changes in this commit.

strengths: Clean duck-typed broker protocol (start/publish/add_client/remove_client/client_exists/subscribe_client/unsubscribe_client) lets Redis and in-memory implementations swap cleanly
SQLite append-only MessageStore with autoincrement IDs and descending list is simple and correctly locked
Self-contained with no third-party dependencies added, keeping the worktree portable
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally useful integration session (persistence + broker abstraction) whose hand-rolled RESP client and silent Redis-to-memory fallback introduce avoidable protocol/availability debt, while conventions hold at the measured 0.83 with violations confined to test_app.py.

problems.description: Leaky abstraction: NotificationServer.handler() relies on an isinstance() check against WebSocketTransport and calls self._transport.handler(), but handler is NOT part of the BaseTransport ABC interface — a new transport backend must reimplement server glue rather than being covered by the contract.

Client state now lives in two locks (server _clients_lock for channels/removal plus transport _clients_lock) after the refactor split; ownership of _remove_client vs transport cleanup is implicit and easy to get wrong in a future transport.

WebSocketTransport.broadcast snapshots client_ids under lock then releases it before asyncio.gather, so a client that disconnects between snapshot and send is still targeted (handled via return_exceptions, but a benign TOCTOU race).
The diff adds +15 functions/+2 classes of transport logic with no visible test coverage for WebSocketTransport or the transport factory.

strengths: Clean strategy/ABC abstraction: transport selection via TRANSPORT env + _create_transport factory cleanly separates connection management from broker/message routing
Server no longer owns the transport-specific client dict — responsibility split is genuinely better and removes duplicated broadcast/disconnect logic
Thread-safety preserved: reentrant RLock and lock-free snapshot/release ordering avoid deadlock while keeping dict access consistent
Consistent style: full type hints, docstrings on the abstract contract, tuple return for client_ids, failure-aware send_message/broadcast returning delivery status
Backward compatible: existing handler()/client_ids/public API surface retained for the websocket path
commit_reviews.summary: A solid dependency-inversion refactor that introduces a well-typed BaseTransport contract and removes duplicated client management from NotificationServer, with only minor design smells (handler not on the ABC, dual locking) and no new convention violations — note the 0.83 convention score is driven by pre-existing test_app.py lint findings untouched by this diff.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +25 for the diff size: rate-limit and TTL-cleanup policy logic are embedded directly in NotificationServer/_handle_message rather than isolated in a dedicated concern; a separate RateLimiter/RetentionPolicy class would keep the server thin.
close() cancels _cleanup_task but there is no visible wiring to server shutdown in the diff — if unregistered, the cleanup task and per-client rate_limits dict entries live for the process lifetime.

delete_older_than applies datetime(timestamp) on every row, defeating the new (channel, timestamp, id) index for the retention scan; timezone-aware ISO strings compared via SQLite datetime() may also normalize offsets inconsistently.
Fixed-window rate limit hardcodes window_seconds=60 at the call site and counts every inbound message type; fine at 100/min but the policy is implicit rather than a named constant.

strengths: Both InMemoryBroker and RedisBroker gain the identical increment_rate_limit interface with the Redis path correctly forwarding to the fallback broker — the broker abstraction is extended consistently, not duplicated.
parse_qs replaces the hand-rolled query-string split, fixing URL-encoding and repeated-key edge cases on the /messages and /history endpoints.
history() uses the limit+1 fetch to compute has_more without an extra COUNT query — solid pagination, and the composite index (channel, timestamp, id) backs the ORDER BY.
Lifecycle refactor (_start_broker -> start) is idempotent and guarded, with close() properly cancelling the background task via asyncio.CancelledError handling.
Strong conventions: snake_case methods, type hints on all new public signatures, existing lock/connection context-manager patterns reused, controlled (non-injected) WHERE construction.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean cross-cutting session that fits the existing broker and store abstractions well (rate limiting, paginated history, TTL retention); the mild debt is policy logic inline in the server and an index-defeating retention scan, while the measured 0.83 convention score understates the app code, which is uniformly idiomatic — the two violations land in test_app.py rather than the app itself.

compounding_issues: Monolithic single-file app.py grew from 146 to 636 lines with no module split; the health_response method silently became an ad-hoc HTTP router for 5+ endpoints (query parsing bolted on in S5) instead of a dispatch structure.

Channel subscription state is duplicated — kept both locally (_channels) and in the broker (Redis sets / shared class dicts) — while routing only ever uses the local copy; the broker-side membership is redundant and, in the Redis path, never cleaned on disconnect (remove_client only HDELs the clients hash, so channel sets accumulate stale members).

Hand-rolled Redis RESP client opens a fresh TCP connection per command via _execute() (no connection reuse, no pipelining) — inefficient and a large body of low-level protocol code to maintain that a standard client would provide for free.

InMemoryBroker uses class-level mutable state (subscribers, clients, channel_members, rate_limits) shared across instances — intentional for the cross-server test but a footgun where rate-limit counters and client registries leak between logically independent servers in the same process.
Rate-limit check in S5 runs before message validation, so subscribe/unsubscribe messages and even malformed input all consume the per-client quota.
Direct-message delivery was rerouted in S3 to round-trip through the pub/sub broker even for single-instance operation, adding latency and coupling routing to broker availability.
key_decisions: Uniform message envelope {type, payload, timestamp} with a strict MESSAGE_TYPES allowlist and centralized invalid-message error handling (seeded, reinforced in S1).
Channel-based pub/sub model in S2: subscribe/unsubscribe message types, channel-scoped broadcasts, plus HTTP introspection endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers).

S3's hand-rolled Redis RESP pub/sub client with a memory:// in-memory fallback broker — zero third-party dependencies, enabling multi-instance fan-out and deterministic tests at the cost of maintainability.
SQLite append-only MessageStore (S3) for history, later extended (S5) with a channel-filtered, since-aware, paginated /history endpoint with has_more + a messages index.
S4's BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport abstraction, which cleanly extracted the client registry/send/broadcast machinery out of NotificationServer and reduced coupling.

S5's cross-cutting operational controls: per-client rate limiting (Redis INCR+EXPIRE / in-memory sliding window) and TTL-based message expiry via a background cleanup task with start()/close() lifecycle management.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. S1 established a solid, well-tested WebSocket core; S2 added a clean, focused channels feature with matching tests; S3 was the ambitious integration jump (SQLite history + pub/sub broker) that delivered real capability but also introduced most of the later structural debt (monolith growth, dual channel state, hand-rolled RESP); S4 showed disciplined architectural discipline by extracting a transport abstraction that genuinely reduced coupling; S5 delivered production-minded cross-cutting polish (rate limiting, message TTL expiry, history API). Test coverage grew from 4 to 11 tests with each feature accompanied by tests, and no session regressed prior functionality — though the accumulated debt from S3 was never paid down.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting arc that improved in quality each session, with clean abstractions and growing test coverage, but accumulated real structural debt (monolithic file, redundant broker channel state, hand-rolled Redis client) during the ambitious integration session.
